title: Micah 7:8–20
context: The city, speaking as one person, tells her enemy not to rejoice, confessing that she has sinned and must bear the LORD’s indignation “until he pleads my case,” and trusting that “the LORD will be a light to me.” The prophet foresees walls rebuilt and people coming from Assyria and Egypt, prays, “Shepherd your people with your staff,” and hears the LORD answer, “I will show them marvelous things,” before the book closes with the confession, “Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity,” and the hope that the LORD will keep his oath to Abraham and Jacob. Both traditions read 7:18–20 as shared confession of God’s mercy, and questions about the pardoned remnant and election point to the existing box at Romans 11:5 rather than a new one.

verses.text: Don’t rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise.” Arminian readers note that Zion, personified, now speaks.

The enemy is not named and may be one of the nations that humbled Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hold the identity of the enemy lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions hear the confidence “the LORD will be a light to me” as hope in darkness.

verses.text: I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my case and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light. I will see his righteousness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my case.” Arminian readers note the honest confession of sin.

Zion accepts discipline while trusting God’s vindication.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see repentance joined to hope in God’s righteousness.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the one who disciplines is also the one who will “bring me out to the light.”

verses.text: Then my enemy will see it, and shame will cover her who said to me, “Where is the LORD your God?” My eyes will see her. Now she will be trodden down like the mire of the streets.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then my enemy will see it, and shame will cover her who said to me, “Where is the LORD your God?”” Arminian readers note the reversal of mockery.

The enemy’s taunt is answered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God vindicating his name before those who scorned it (cf. Ps 42:10).

Shared ground: both traditions read the image of the enemy trodden down soberly, as poetry about vindication rather than a call to revenge.

verses.text: A day to build your walls! In that day, he will extend your boundary.
verses.arminianNotes:
“A day to build your walls! In that day, he will extend your boundary.” Arminian readers note the promise of rebuilding.

The walls that fell will rise again.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see restoration following judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as hope for a restored Zion, without fixing a single historical moment for its fulfillment.

verses.text: In that day they will come to you from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt even to the River, and from sea to sea, and mountain to mountain.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In that day they will come to you from Assyria and the cities of Egypt.” Arminian readers note the gathering from distant lands.

The scope runs “from sea to sea, and mountain to mountain.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the wide reach of the coming restoration.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of gathering, and both note the related vision of nations streaming to Zion in Micah 4:1–2, named without harmonizing.

verses.text: Yet the land will be desolate because of those who dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Yet the land will be desolate because of those who dwell therein, for the fruit of their doings.” Arminian readers note that judgment still comes before restoration.

The desolation is linked to what people have done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the seriousness of sin even within a passage of hope.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that hope does not erase accountability, and both read the verse as a sober note within the promise.

verses.text: Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock of your heritage, who dwell by themselves in a forest. Let them feed in the middle of fertile pasture land, in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old.
verses.arminianNotes:
The prophet prays, “Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock of your heritage.” Arminian readers note the request for the LORD’s care.

Bashan and Gilead were known for rich pasture.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as the shepherd of his people (cf. Ps 23:1).

Shared ground: both traditions read the prayer as longing for renewed blessing “as in the days of old.”

verses.text: “As in the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show them marvelous things.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD answers, “As in the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt, I will show them marvelous things.” Arminian readers note that the exodus is the pattern for future deliverance.

The prayer is heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s past faithfulness as the ground of future hope.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the God who redeemed Israel from Egypt will act again for his people.

verses.text: The nations will see and be ashamed of all their might. They will lay their hand on their mouth. Their ears will be deaf.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The nations will see and be ashamed of all their might. They will lay their hand on their mouth.” Arminian readers note the humbling of the nations.

Their strength is shown to be nothing before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s glory displayed before the world.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the nations falling silent before the LORD’s mighty acts.

verses.text: They will lick the dust like a serpent. Like crawling things of the earth, they will come trembling out of their dens. They will come with fear to the LORD our God, and will be afraid because of you.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They will come with fear to the LORD our God, and will be afraid because of you.” Arminian readers note that the nations turn toward the LORD in fear.

The imagery of dust and crawling pictures deep humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the nations brought low before God.

Shared ground: both traditions read the strong imagery soberly as a picture of humbled pride, and both note that the nations come “to the LORD our God.”

verses.text: Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage? He doesn’t retain his anger forever, because he delights in loving kindness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Who is a God like you, who pardons iniquity, and passes over the disobedience of the remnant of his heritage?” Arminian readers hear an echo of Exodus 15:11 and 34:6–7.

Micah’s own name is often linked to the question of who is like the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a confession that God “delights in loving kindness.”

Shared ground: both traditions confess God’s pardoning mercy together.

verses.text: He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.” Arminian readers note the vivid pictures of forgiveness.

Sin is defeated and removed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the completeness of God’s pardon (cf. Ps 103:12).

Shared ground: both traditions rejoice that God does not merely overlook sin but removes it, and both may hear an echo of the exodus at the sea.

verses.text: You will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will give truth to Jacob, and mercy to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.” Arminian readers note that the book ends with God’s faithfulness to his promises.

The oath recalls Genesis 22:16–17.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the covenant promises grounded in God’s sworn word (cf. Luke 1:72–73).

Shared ground: both traditions close Micah with a shared confession of the LORD’s truth and mercy to his people.
